Further information: [Music of *Star Wars*](/wiki/Music_of_Star_Wars "Music of Star Wars")

[John Williams](/wiki/John_Williams "John Williams") composed the soundtracks for the nine episodic films. He stated he would retire from the franchise with *The Rise of Skywalker*,[[208]](#cite_note-213) but he composed a theme for Obi-Wan Kenobi for the [miniseries](/wiki/Obi-Wan_Kenobi_(miniseries) "Obi-Wan Kenobi (miniseries)") and Han Solo's theme for *Solo: A Star Wars Story*.[[209]](#cite_note-SoloScore-214) Williams also created the main theme for *[Galaxy's Edge](/wiki/Star_Wars:_Galaxy%27s_Edge "Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge")*.[[210]](#cite_note-215)

Several other composers worked on other soundtracks, including [John Powell](/wiki/John_Powell_(composer) "John Powell (composer)") (*Obi-Wan Kenobi*), [Michael Giacchino](/wiki/Michael_Giacchino "Michael Giacchino") (*Rogue One*),[[209]](#cite_note-SoloScore-214) and [Ludwig Göransson](/wiki/Ludwig_G%C3%B6ransson "Ludwig Göransson") (*[The Mandalorian](/wiki/The_Mandalorian "The Mandalorian")*).[[211]](#cite_note-216)

[James Bond](/wiki/James_Bond_(literary_character) "James Bond (literary character)") is a fictional character created by British novelist [Ian Fleming](/wiki/Ian_Fleming "Ian Fleming") in 1953. A British secret agent working for [MI6](/wiki/Secret_Intelligence_Service "Secret Intelligence Service") under the codename 007, Bond has been [portrayed on film](/wiki/Portrayal_of_James_Bond_in_film "Portrayal of James Bond in film") in twenty-seven productions by actors [Sean Connery](/wiki/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery"), [David Niven](/wiki/David_Niven "David Niven"), [George Lazenby](/wiki/George_Lazenby "George Lazenby"), [Roger Moore](/wiki/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore"), [Timothy Dalton](/wiki/Timothy_Dalton "Timothy Dalton"), [Pierce Brosnan](/wiki/Pierce_Brosnan "Pierce Brosnan"), and [Daniel Craig](/wiki/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig"). [Eon Productions](/wiki/Eon_Productions "Eon Productions"), which now holds the adaptation rights to all of [Fleming's Bond novels](/wiki/List_of_James_Bond_novels_and_short_stories "List of James Bond novels and short stories"), made all but two entries in the film series.[[1]](#cite_note-Poliakoff-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Shprintz:Variety-2)

In 1961, producers [Albert R. Broccoli](/wiki/Albert_R._Broccoli "Albert R. Broccoli") and [Harry Saltzman](/wiki/Harry_Saltzman "Harry Saltzman") purchased the filming rights to Fleming's novels.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChapman20095-3) They founded Eon Productions and, with financial backing by [United Artists](/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists"), produced *[Dr. No](/wiki/Dr._No_(film) "Dr. No (film)")*, directed by [Terence Young](/wiki/Terence_Young_(director) "Terence Young (director)") and featuring Connery as Bond.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChapman20

Definitions of the boundary between Asia and Oceania

The border between Asia and [Oceania](/wiki/Oceania "Oceania") is usually placed somewhere in the [Indonesian Archipelago](/wiki/Indonesian_Archipelago "Indonesian Archipelago"), specifically in [Eastern Indonesia](/wiki/Eastern_Indonesia "Eastern Indonesia"). The [Wallace Line](/wiki/Wallace_Line "Wallace Line") separates the Asian and [Wallacea](/wiki/Wallacea "Wallacea") biogeographical realms, a transition zone of deep water straits between the Asian and Australian continental shelves. [Weber's Line](/wiki/Weber%27s_Line "Weber's Line") split the region in two with regard to the balance of fauna between Asian origin or Australo-Papuan origin.[[38]](#cite_note-Simpson-1977-40) Wallacea's eastern boundary with [Sahul](/wiki/Australia_(continent) "Australia (continent)") is represented by the [Lydekker's Line](/wiki/Richard_Lydekker "Richard Lydekker").[[39]](#cite_note-41)[[40]](#cite_note-42) The [Maluku Islands](/wiki/Maluku_Islands "Maluku Islands") (except the [Aru Islands](/wiki/Aru_Islands_Regency "Aru Islands Regency")) are often considered to lie on the border of southeast Asia, with the Aru Islands and [Western New Guinea](/wiki/Western_New_Guinea "Western New Guinea"), to the east of the Lydekker's Line, being wholly part of Oceania, as both lie on the Australian continental plate.[[38]](#cite_note-Simpson-1977-40) Culturally, the Wallacea region denoted the transition between [Austronesian](/wiki/Austronesian_people "Austronesian people") and [Melanesian people](/wiki/Melanesian_people "Melanesian people"), with varying degrees of intermixing between the two. [Christopher Columbus Langdell](/wiki/Christopher_Columbus_Langdell "Christopher Columbus Langdell"), an influential dean of [Harvard Law School](/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School") from 1875 to 1890

The establishment of Harvard Law School in 1817 was made possible by a 1779 bequest from [Isaac Royall Jr.](/wiki/Isaac_Royall_Jr. "Isaac Royall Jr."); it is the oldest continuously operating law school in the nation.[[129]](#cite_note-Gershman-130) It was a small operation and grew slowly. By 1827, it was down to one faculty member. [Nathan Dane](/wiki/Nathan_Dane "Nathan Dane"), a prominent alumnus, endowed the Dane Professorship of Law and insisted that it be given to then Supreme Court Justice [Joseph Story](/wiki/Joseph_Story "Joseph Story"). For a while, the school was called Dane Law School.[[130]](#cite_note-131) Story's belief in the need for an elite law school based on merit and dedicated to public service helped build the school's reputation at the time. Enrollment remained low as academic legal education was considered to be of little added benefit to apprenticeships in legal practice.

Radical reform came in the 1870s, under Dean [Christopher Columbus Langdell](/wiki/Christopher_Columbus_Langdell "Christopher Columbus Langdell") (1826–1906).[[131]](#cite_note-132) Its new curriculum set the national standard and was copied widely in the United States. Langdell developed the [case method](/wiki/Casebook_method "Casebook method") of teaching law, based on his belief that law could be studied as a "science" gave university legal education a reason for being distinct from vocational preparation. The school introduced a first-year curriculum that was widely imitated, based on classes in [contracts](/wiki/Contra

fanoutqa_006213.x:
Supreme Court of the United States :: Membership :: Retired justices :: chunk_0018
There are two living retired justices of the Supreme Court of the United States: Anthony Kennedy and Stephen Breyer. As retired justices, they no longer participate in the work of the Supreme Court, but may be designated for temporary assignments to sit on lower federal courts, usually the [United States Courts of Appeals](/wiki/United_States_Courts_of_Appeals "United States Courts of Appeals"). Such assignments are formally made by the chief justice, on request of the [chief judge](/wiki/Chief_judge_(United_States) "Chief judge (United States)") of the lower court and with the consent of the retired justice. The status of a retired justice is analogous to that of a circuit or district court judge who has taken [senior status](/wiki/Senior_status "Senior status"), and eligibility of a Supreme Court justice to assume retired status (rather than simply resign from the bench) is governed by the same age and service criteria.

In recent times, justices tend to strategically plan their decisions to leave the bench with personal, institutional, ideological, partisan, and political factors playing a role.[[168]](#cite_note-168)[[169]](#cite_note-169) The fear of mental decline and death often motivates justices to step down. The desire to maximize the court's strength and legitimacy through one retirement at a time, when the court is in recess and during non-presidential election years suggests a concern for institutional health. Finally, especially in recent decades, many justices have timed their departure to coincide with a philosophically compatible president holding office, to ensure that a like-minded successor would be appointed.[[170]](#cite_note-170)[[171]](#cite_note-171)

Later that same year, they would [trade veteran running back](/wiki/Herschel_Walker_trade "Herschel Walker trade") [Herschel Walker](/wiki/Herschel_Walker "Herschel Walker") to the [Minnesota Vikings](/wiki/Minnesota_Vikings "Minnesota Vikings") for five veteran players and eight draft choices. In March 2023, Saudi Aramco announced that they had seen record profits of $161 billion as prices of petrol soared following the COVID-19 pandemic. The figures eclipsed the numbers posted by ExxonMobil and Shell, who reported $55.7 and $39.9 billion in profit respectively.[[91]](#cite_note-91) In March 2023, Saudi Aramco announced it was going to acquire a 10% stake in China's Rongsheng Petrochemical Co. Ltd, with an estimated purchase price of $3.6 billion, and plans to build a new refining and petrochemical complex in northeast China through a joint venture.[[92]](#cite_note-92)

In September 2023, it was announced that Saudi Aramco had reached an agreement with the [Latin American](/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") [private equity fund](/wiki/Private_equity_fund "Private equity fund"), Southern Cross Group to acquire the [Santiago](/wiki/Santiago "Santiago")-headquartered fuel retailer, Esmax Distribución SPA, operator of [Petrobras](/wiki/Petrobras "Petrobras")-branded service stations in Chile. The acquisition marks Saudi Aramco's entry into the [South American](/wiki/South_America "South America") fuel retailing market,[[93]](#cite_note-93) and beginning in May 2024, the 300 Petrobras service stations in Chile will be gradually converted to Aramco service stations.[[94]](#cite_note-94)[[95]](#cite_note-95) In September 2023, Indian engineering and construction giant Larsen & Toubro (L&T) signed a contract with Saudi Aramco. The Jafoor unconventional gas development expansion project in Saudi Arabia where L&T will build a gas processing plant and major processing facilities is worth $2.9 billion.[[96]](#cite_note-96) In December 2023, Saudi Aramco acquired 40% shares in Gas & Oil Pakistan for an undisclosed amount.[[97]](#cite_note-97)
